# PREFACE.

ALTHOUGH, after reading the book recently published against us by Dr. <term>Koelman<note>Jacobus Koelman (1632–1695) was a influential Dutch Reformed minister who became a fierce critic of the Labadist movement, the radical pietist group to which the author of this text belongs.</note></term>, I believed that something ought to be answered, I nevertheless remained in doubt for some time as to whether I should do so. Many assured us from various sides that the author had done himself more harm than he was capable of doing to those against whom he wrote, and that there was no appearance that souls who had any knowledge of the truths that God makes us profess, and of the life that we lead through His grace, would be brought to wavering by such a writing, or hindered or obstructed in their attraction to this Work of the Lord, and the union of their hearts with the same. 

And since the manner in which Dr. Koelman chose to declare himself against us is somewhat strange, and because answering him with all the force that the truth would allow—even grant us to use—would only embitter him further and cause him to write again in a way that would be even less edifying; so I can say that I have had some difficulty in arriving at what we are now doing; and that for my part I would just as gladly have followed the advice of some of our friends, who counseled us not to spend our time refuting things that did not seem to require it. 

Nevertheless, since on that occasion I felt once again the desire arising in my heart—which I have had for a long time—to treat more fully and explicitly certain points and truths that the Lord makes us embrace, and which need to be better known; and that some of our friends, and in particular Dr. <term>Copper<note>Likely Johannes Copper, a physician and associate of the Labadist community who defended their views.</note></term>, wrote to me that they believed it would be good for something to come to light against the book of Dr. Koelman, and against the Letters that have been added there to give it more weight and authority, I thought that these two matters together <note>original: "te famen", likely "together" based on the catchword</note>

And our only desire, by His grace, is that the truth alone be followed, to the glory of His name and for the true good of His people.

Although **Water-baptism** does not save us, as Peter says <note>A reference to 1 Peter 3:21, where the Apostle Peter explains that baptism is not merely the washing of dirt from the body, but an appeal to God for a good conscience.</note>, it is nevertheless highly necessary that its use be properly regulated, and that its administration happen according to the truth of the Gospel and the foundation of the <term>New Covenant<note>The theological concept that God has established a new relationship with humanity through Jesus Christ, replacing the Old Testament Law.</note></term>, of which it is the sign and seal, as is the **Lord’s Supper**. Both signify and seal great and highly important matters: it is therefore right that one takes care not to seal them carelessly, or without having sufficient reason for doing so. Otherwise, one gradually debases the truths of Christianity and makes them contemptible; one loses and takes away the living impression that one ought to have of them, and one imagines that nothing is easier or more common than being a Christian—just as there is nothing more common than being baptized, and nothing easier than receiving baptism. For certainly, if **Baptism** were not administered except to those for whom there is reason to testify that they share in the things signified to them by baptism, would that not open the eyes of many people who now consider themselves to be Christians simply because they are baptized? Such people are found not only among the Roman-minded <note>Those adhering to the Roman Catholic Church.</note>, or among those called Lutherans, who explicitly establish this as a doctrine; but there are also many among the <term>Reformed<note>The Dutch Reformed Church (Gereformeerde Kerk), which followed Calvinist theology.</note></term>, as <term>D. What we propose in this book can serve to help and heal them, if it pleases the Lord to pour out His Divine blessing upon it. And we believe that the embracing of the truth contained therein would greatly restore the holiness of this Sacrament, and make its practice much more useful and beneficial than it is and can be now, when it is practiced according to the ordinary custom <note>original: "ordinaren fleur"; referring to the common, fashionable practice of the state church rather than a strict biblical one.</note>. Several Treatises that follow will, if the Lord wills, explain various other matters in the same way, and show, as I hope, that we are better grounded in them than D. Koelman thinks and wishes to make those believe into whose minds and hearts he would like to instill all his prejudices and groundless thoughts.

In the meantime, following the **Doctrine of Baptism**, one will find general Remarks on his book, where one will see in few words the explanation and clarification of many things that he has seen fit to confuse and obscure, as well as the proper answer to those points that seemed most to require it. Firstly, we believe we have reason to complain about the manner and way in which Reverend Koelman proceeds against this **Work of the Lord** <note>The author's term for the Labadist community and their spiritual reforms.</note>. There are, I believe, few who would not agree that he could and should have been more restrained and more just in what he wanted to say or write against us. And he himself would surely see that, if he were not so accustomed to a style of writing and speaking that is somewhat bitter and excessive. He thinks it is all zeal, and zeal for the truth. But must that zeal not be pure? And would his zeal not be greater if it were more modest and moderate, and less mixed with that fire which is natural to him, and which therefore certainly needs to be purified? I wish from my heart that he would pay heed to this, and I can say with truth that it is out of the love I bear for his soul—for which it is known I have had a special tenderness—having often been grieved that, through adherence to his own thoughts and certain prejudices taken over from others, he allowed himself to be carried away to speak of this Work of the Lord as he has done.

when one reads our remarks on his Letter, one will undoubtedly be surprised that he often speaks with as much assurance of things that are not true as of those that are. This is a notable defect, especially when it results in wronging one's neighbor and thinking ill of him for things of which he is not guilty. We request that he pay heed to this in the future.

Among the things he says of <term>Mr. de Labadie<note>Jean de Labadie (1610–1674), a former Jesuit priest who converted to the Reformed faith and later founded a communal pietist sect known as the Labadists.</note></term>, of whom he frequently speaks in a very unworthy and unbecoming manner, I cannot refrain from pointing out here that he cannot be cleared of the charge of rash judgment when he dares to say so bluntly that this faithful servant of God—who now rests in the bosom of His glory—was **outside of Christ** <note>original: "buyten Christus was"; a severe theological claim suggesting that Labadie was not among the saved or "elect" during his transition between faiths.</note> when he, leaving the <term>Roman Catholics<note>original: "Roomſch-geſinde."</note></term> (whose errors, abuses, and idolatry he had fought as faithfully and courageously as he had their corruptions and sins), joined himself outwardly to the Reformed Church at **Montauban** and publicly embraced its doctrine. This doctrine he had already believed, confessed, and defended in his heart for a long time, having often been in danger of life and limb for it, and seeing the greatest in all **France**, both secular and ecclesiastical, rise up against him. The Reformed ministers in **Picardy** who publicly prayed for him in their churches as one of His servants who suffered in the midst of his enemies for His sake, were far from the opinion of <term>Reverend Koelman<note>original: "D. Koelman."</note></term>, and took care not to view him as being "outside of Christ." I also know that he was received at Montauban as a man of God, to whom they were quickly prepared to give the **right hand of fellowship** <note>A traditional gesture of formal recognition and partnership in Christian ministry, based on Galatians 2:9.</note>, after having seen the graces and gifts that God had placed in him, the light that He had shared with him, and the fiery zeal with which He had caused him to work for the advancement of His cause, and fur-

He will perhaps say that Bernard guarded himself against them; but we can also answer that if he knew how God's wise and faithful guidance was over and around Mr. de Labadie, he would see that this servant of Jesus Christ, by His grace, guarded himself even more against them.

Was there then no people of God in Babylon <note>A common biblical metaphor used by Reformers to refer to the Roman Catholic Church, drawing from the Book of Revelation's command to "come out of her, my people."</note>, when the Lord let His fine voice be heard, and commanded them to go out from there? Would <term>D. Koelman<note>Jacobus Koelman (1632–1695), a Dutch minister and prominent critic of the Labadist movement.</note></term> really dare to hold all those who lived under the **Papacy** before the Reformation as idolaters, or as estranged from Christ? And does he not believe that after that time the Lord could still have kept some remnant of His true people under the same, whom He did not wish to pull out immediately—especially when He wanted to use some of them to testify against it? He showed that He had exactly this intention for His faithful servant <term>Mr. de Labadie<note>Jean de Labadie (1610–1674), the former Jesuit who became a famous Reformed preacher and later founded the Labadist community.</note></term>. 

If D. Koelman would cast his eye on what <term>Mr. Pajon<note>Claude Pajon (1626–1685), a French theologian known for his views on grace and providence.</note></term>, a minister in **France**, recently wrote in his refutation of the book called *Legitimate Prejudices against the Calvinists* <note>original: *Préjugez legitimes contre les Calvinistes*, a famous polemical work by Pierre Nicole.</note> pages 127, 128, 129, he would see there how one had to receive Mr. de Labadie when he came over from the **Roman Catholics** to the **Reformed**, and how his calling to the pastoral office had as little need of being renewed as his baptism; indeed less, one could say, if the matter is well-taken and viewed more in its foundation than in its external circumstances. 

Since D. Koelman has grieved and wounded the hearts of many who, with good reason, have a tender love and high esteem for that faithful servant of Jesus Christ, it is only fair that we have dwelled a bit on what he said about him, and that we admonish him that henceforth he should no longer speak and write of him as he has done in his book against us. ...a certain simplicity and freedom that the Lord gives them, which the ordinary Believers do not have. ...has drawn [them] out of the love for the world and for all that is in it, and whom He has united and made one in Jesus Christ for time and eternity; this clearly shows that His Spirit was as much, indeed more than ever, in and with this His **Servant**, whom He used so particularly as an instrument for the formation of the **Work** that He, through His grace, wished to establish among us. Thus, it is very wrongful for <term>D. If Reverend Koelman does not believe it, I shall show it to him through the opinion that Reverend Copper had of it, as he testifies in a letter to me from April 6th of this year: with which I shall end this preface.

> *We have*, he says, *read Reverend Koelman’s Book in Düsseldorf with sadness, and wondered at his blindness, and his perverse and wicked procedures, by which he hardens the godless, gives weapons into the hands of enemies, binds the prisoners, strengthens the lovers of the world, confuses the weak, makes the resistors rejoice, confounds the Old and New Testaments, and unites flesh and spirit, light and darkness, the world and the Church. So it goes when one is blind and dim regarding the <term>Fundamental Truths</term> <note>original: "Hooft-waerheden," referring to the essential doctrines of the faith.</note>, and holds that darkness for light, and wishes to be zealous for that imagined light. Just as that darkness is evil, so also that zeal, with all that comes forth from it, cannot be good nor divine, but must be evil and carnal, just as experience here teaches.*

<margin>The proposal regarding the baptism of children is certainly very useful.</margin> ...for the good of God's church, [they] wish that—especially in these times in which deception and corruption have generally taken the upper hand—the administration of Baptism were delayed until the children gave some evidence of the fear and love of God, and were to some extent instructed in the knowledge of the mysteries of Jesus Christ, and of what He absolutely requires of those who call themselves **Christians** and His **Disciples**.

IX. It is not that these **godly persons** <note>In this context, "godly persons" refers to the "vroomen" or Pietists within the Dutch Reformed Church who emphasized personal, felt experience of faith over formal ritual.</note>, both **Pastors** <note>original: "Herders" (Shepherds), a common term for ministers.</note> and others, do not acknowledge that **holy Baptism** belongs and may be administered to all those of whom one has a good foundation to believe that they are partakers of the grace of Jesus Christ; and it is also not that they do not agree that this grace is communicated to various children according to the election and the good pleasure of God: But as that is not ordinary, and on the contrary very rare, and as almost nothing [of grace] is seen, while the opposite [of grace] is seen a great deal when the children come of age; therefore it is also their opinion that it would be much safer and better to wait until one had some certain and more substantial <term>re-eele</term> <note>Meaning "real" or "demonstrable" in a legal or theological sense.</note> signs of the state of their grace and **regeneration** <note>original: "wedergeboorte," referring to the spiritual rebirth required for salvation.</note>, so that one might also, when they were baptized, be able to instruct them at the same time in the obligations of Baptism, and teach what **Christ** requires of all those who are baptized.

# Doctrine of Baptism

Thus, in the beginning of the Reformation, there were entire Churches / who almost preferred to postpone presenting children for baptism / as much as others preferred to do so immediately / keeping themselves satisfied (they say *) that the fathers presented the same to Jesus Christ the Mediator and Savior through the prayers of the Church, confessing that they stood in need of His blood and the power thereof. ### RESOLUTION of the objections which are or can be brought against the preceding Teaching.

<margin>I. Objection, taken from Circumcision.</margin>
I. <margin>Circumcision and Baptism must not be compared regarding the time of their administration.</margin>

# Doctrine of Baptism

[The chur]ches of Africa, with their pastors living in the third century, believed that everyone who had been baptized by heretics had to be baptized again; and their practice was consistent with their teaching. But the other churches, which held a different view, did not excommunicate them for it, nor did they separate from them: for they did not look so much at what they did, as at the foundation upon which they acted, which differed greatly from the basis of the **Donatists** <note>A schismatic group in North Africa that arose in the 4th century; they believed the church must be pure and that sacraments performed by "fallen" priests were invalid.</note>, whose practice shortly thereafter was the same, but was founded on their **schism** <note>original: *scheuring*; a formal split or division within the church.</note>, which was undertaken for trivial causes and mere questions of fact that were themselves found to be false, and was accompanied by violence, treachery, and a gross ignorance. 

This led them so far as to believe that there were no **elect** <note>original: *uytverkoorne*; those chosen by God for salvation.</note> or holy ones except in Africa alone, and within their own assemblies or congregations. Therefore, they rebaptized—even by force—everyone they could draw to their side, and thereby made **rebaptism** <note>original: *herdoopen*.</note> something very evil and criminal, even though it had been tolerated in **Cyprian** <note>Saint Cyprian (c. 210–258 AD), the Bishop of Carthage who famously argued that heretical baptisms were void, necessitating rebaptism upon entering the true Church.</note> and all the other bishops of Africa because they did it on different grounds; they only rebaptized those who came over to them from the heretics, whom they believed could not lawfully baptize nor were authorized by God to do so. From this, it is reasonable to conclude for our cause that

### Doctrine of Baptism

...which God made with **Abraham**, was not a simple renewal or application of the **Covenant of Grace** <note>In Reformed theology, the Covenant of Grace is God's eternal plan to save humanity through faith, spanning both the Old and New Testaments.</note> to him; but that it moreover contained, as it were, the seed of the **two general Covenants** which God intended to establish with the two peoples—the old and the new—of which **Abraham** was appointed as Head and Father through this **Covenant** that God made with him. # G E N E R A L
### Remarks and Considerations regarding the Book of <term>Dominie Koelman<note>Jacobus Koelman (1632–1695) was a prominent Dutch Reformed minister and a leading figure in the 'Nadere Reformatie' or Further Reformation, known for his prolific writing and controversial stances on church liturgy.</note></term>, and particularly concerning the supposed errors with which it has pleased him to charge us.

In these Remarks we shall principally show that Dominie Koelman ascribes many things to us which we do not hold, nor have ever held or believed. Several points which he has misunderstood, and consequently also poorly represented, we shall explain and clarify. And some others that require it, we shall briefly defend and account for; pointing, for the rest, either to the Books where they have already been sufficiently proven, or to the <term>Treatises<note>The author refers to a series of pamphlets or doctrinal essays common in 17th-century religious debate.</note></term> that are yet to follow regarding the matters that shall need it, such as the subject of **Baptism**, which we have explained in this Treatise, as it still seemed to require further attention. This is what we propose for ourselves in the following Considerations or remarks, in which one shall find—

But He who justifies, the same deifies, because by justifying He makes them sons of God. For He gave them power to become sons of God. If we are made sons of God, we are also made gods: but this is of the grace of the one adopting, not of the nature of the one generating. For the only Son of God is God, and with the Father one God, our Lord and Savior Jesus Christ, in the beginning the Word, and the Word was with God, the Word was God. Others who become gods, become so by His grace; they are not born of His substance to be what He is, but that by His benefit they might come to Him, and be co-heirs with Christ.... To the gods of the gentiles, He is a terror as to demons: to the gods made by Himself, He is lovable as to sons.... To those for whom He is lovable, they are sons: to those for whom He is a terror, they are not sons. To those for whom He is lovable, He made them gods: those for whom He is a terror, He proves they are not gods. For these [the believers] become gods; the others are only thought to be gods. Truth makes these gods; error imagines those. See also the letter of Fulgentius <note>Fulgentius of Ruspe (c. 467–533) was an African bishop and a staunch follower of Augustine's theology.</note> to Ferrandus concerning the Baptism of a dying Ethiopian, chapter 3.</margin>

# General Observations
<meta>catchword: &</meta>

<margin>I was stunned, and I stood astonished, when I saw the manifold profanity, heterodoxy, and blasphemy gathered into that book; and that there was but one Theologian (but truly how great a man, concerning whose virtues, gifts, and graces I think it better to be silent than to say little: nor do I have such power or abundance of speech that I can express in words what I feel about him. Therefore, imitating Timanthes in depicting Iphigenia as she was about to perish at the altar, what I cannot express with the brush of my pen, I will cover with a veil; I will say this, which no one except the most shameless could deny: that for many years he was a faithful worker in the Lord's vineyard, a tireless athlete in the sacred arena, <note>original Latin: "Obstupui, stetiq; attonitus, ubi prophanitatem simul & heterodoxiã ac blasphemiam multiplicẽ vidi in eum librum congestam; quodq; nõ nisi unus Theologus (At vir sanè quam magnus, de cujus virtutibus, donis & gratiis tacere potius puto, quam pauca dicere: nec est ea mihi dicendi vis aut copia, ut quæ de ipso sentio, verbis queam exprimere. Quare imitatus Timantẽ in depingenda Iphigenia ad arã periturâ, quod exprimere styli penicillo non possum, velo obtegam; id dicã, quod nullus nisi impudentissimus negare poterit, quod multos annos fidelem in vinea Domini operarium, indefessum in sacra palæstra athletam,"</note></margin>...of God seen in him, felt, and experienced for so long. These words of **<term>D. Koelman</term>**<note>Jacobus Koelman (1632–1695), a Dutch Reformed minister and writer.</note> appear in the preface of his book written in Latin against **<term>Wolzogen</term>**<note>Lodewijk Wolzogen (1633–1690), a professor of theology who engaged in fierce polemics with Labadie.</note>, where he expresses himself thus: I was very displaced and stood amazed when I saw such manifold **<term>profanity</term>**, **<term>heterodoxy</term>**, and **<term>blasphemy</term>**<note>In this context, heterodoxy refers to beliefs that differ from established Church dogma, while profanity and blasphemy suggest a perceived insult to the divine.</note> gathered together in that book, and that there was only one Theologian (namely **Mr. de Labadie**) who set himself against it. # Concerning the Book of **Dr. Koelman**

...all would be lost if one neglected the works that cause time to be spent uselessly and sinfully, and which give the world the means to stray further and further from Jesus—from his example, his word, and his life—and from Christian and Evangelical simplicity. Writing on this matter, I happened to open the <term>Belijdenis-boeken: Confessions</term> <note>original: "Belijdenis-boeken"; referring to the famous autobiographical work by Saint Augustine, *Confessiones*.</note> of **Augustine** to a remarkable passage which I believe would be well-served to include here:

Here we have finally arrived at the last of the errors wrongly attributed to us. And I believe that after what we have said about it, others will not wonder, along with us, that various persons—even some of those who hear and follow **Dr. Koelman** <note>Jacobus Koelman (1632–1695), a Dutch Reformed minister and prominent critic of the Labadists.</note>—have been so dissatisfied with his book; and that there are some (as has been written to us for certain) who are said to have stated that, of the 40 errors he charges us with, they hold more than 30 to be good and pure truths. When we had come into this **Province** <note>Likely Friesland, where the Labadist community moved in 1675.</note>, he wrote a letter to **Mistress van Schurman** <note>Anna Maria van Schurman (1607–1678), a renowned scholar and the most famous member of the Labadist sect.</note>, who was an old friend of his father, in which he presented I know not how many questions to her, with a somewhat masterly air <note>meaning an authoritative or condescending tone</note>, and one that was not very appropriate when writing to such a person as he did. Mistress van Schurman, seeing that this was not a task for a letter requested so suddenly and with such haste, wrote to him about it; and while answering some of his questions, she earnestly showed him that she did not believe herself obligated to satisfy him in the manner he desired, and almost commanded. This he took to heart, and he has shown that he remembered it.

<margin>p. 576.</margin>
In the first cause that **Dr. Brakel** <note>Wilhelmus à Brakel (1635–1711). The page reference likely refers to his influential work, "The Christian’s Reasonable Service."</note> claims to have discovered as to why souls are drawn to us, he asserts that there are those who seek their **sanctification** <term>heyligmaking: the process of being made holy and growing in spiritual character</term> before their **justification** <term>rechtveerdigmaking: the legal act where God declares a sinner righteous through faith</term>; whereas, in his opinion, the latter must first be completed before one comes to the former. As for us, we believe both that those souls—if such exist—would be in error, and that **Dr. Brakel** and those like him deceive themselves if they do not seek **justification** and **sanctification** at the same time, for they go together inseparably. If he thinks otherwise, and acts accordingly, then he certainly misleads souls and merely delays them on their path to God, as we have proven in our *Treatise on Justification*; and we freely admit that we do not teach **godliness** <note>original: "Godsaligheyt"</note> on that basis, which separates those things which are inseparably bound together in Christ and in the believing soul, and which are simultaneously embraced and communicated through His Spirit and grace.

Thus, we are charged with contradictory things that cancel each other out. But the truth is that we are not understood. The soul drawn to God must value her salvation more than all earthly things; but she must love God more than herself and her own salvation, when that salvation is viewed merely as something that makes her happy, or as a benefit coming from God and flowing from His **divine fellowship**. Had they watched, they would have kept the evil ones out—at the very least, out of this garden. Oh, where does it come from? Who knows? We sit now firmly surrounded; they are now inside; it seems much more hopeless to banish them than it would have been to keep them out. We may consider what the causes are here, but one dares not speak of them. 

If the keepers were too weak to resist the enemies and keep them out, how could one repel them now? It is now so peaceful, so easy; there is honor, there is favor, pleasure; everything depends on that. Who could step over this? Here, there should be those surrendered <term>surrendered: "overgegevene," referring to those who have completely submitted their will to God, regardless of worldly cost</term> for the name of the Lord Jesus. 

Tell me, soul, there truly are such people still; why then so hopeless? Yes, but so few; and they say, after all, the spirit must be subject to the spirits of the prophets <note>original: "den geest moet de geesten der Propheten onderworpen zijn." A reference to 1 Corinthians 14:32, frequently cited in the 17th century to emphasize that individual spiritual inspiration must be regulated by the established church order.</note>, and order must be followed. If only the strangers had not instituted laws! But oh, here lies the difficulty: if it were truly the spirit of the prophets, then I could agree to it. There even seems to be collusion by most with the enemies and strangers; how then could they banish them? Where then could we hope? (15)

...indeed [one can] not think of where one should first begin. Yet this concern is not commanded to us, the daughters of Jerusalem <term>daughters of Jerusalem: a biblical metaphor used to represent the community of devout believers or the inner circle of the faithful</term>. It is true—oh no—we acknowledge that; nevertheless, this concerns us, since we also have a Lord to obey, and must be protective of our Bridegroom’s honor. Therefore, at His command, we withdraw from such company where the King’s wrath is also poured out. This would be a constant heartache for us: to see public enemies of our Bridegroom so close by in the inner court, to eat with them, and to perform an Action <term>Action: "Actie," likely referring to the celebration of the Lord’s Supper or a specific communal religious ritual</term> with them. This does not befit the King’s children; they must then go, or we shall depart until they have fled or been driven out. Oh, how sad, if we must depart from where we otherwise could have rejoiced among the festive multitude.

Nevertheless, this gives us courage again, oh our Friend, that You do not dwell in temples made with hands. We will no longer trust in false words, saying, "The Temple of the Lord, the Temple of the Lord, the Temple of the Lord are these" <note>original: "den Tempel des Heeren / den Tempel des Heeren / den Tempel des Heeren zijn dese"; a reference to Jeremiah 7:4, warning against trusting in outward religious institutions while the heart is far from God.</note>.
